e-5727.knowledge_point: Determining Whether Two Events are Mutually Exclusive
e-5727.problem: Given $P(A)=\dfrac{1}{3},$ $P(B)=\dfrac{1}{4},$ and $P(A\cup B)=\dfrac{7}{12},$ determine whether $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events.
e-5727.worked_solution:
To check if $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, we must check that $P(A\cap B) = 0.$

We can calculate $P(A\cap B)$ using the addition law:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ \frac{7}{12} & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{4}-P(A\cap B) \\ P(A\cap B) & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{4}-\frac{7}{12} \\  & =\frac{4+3-7}{12} \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events.

e-5634.knowledge_point: Computing a Probability Involving Mutually Exclusive Events
e-5634.problem: Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events. Given that $P(A)=\dfrac{1}{3}$ and $P(A\cup B) = \dfrac{4}{9},$ find $P(B).$
e-5634.worked_solution:
If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events, then $P(A\cap B) = 0.$ 

Therefore, by the addition law, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B) \\ P(B) & =P(A\cup B)-P(A) \\  & =\frac{4}{9}-\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{4-3}{9} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Given $P(A)=0.25$, $P(B)=0.75$, $P(A\cup B)=0.8$, determine whether  $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events.
after.worked_solution:
To check if $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, we must check that $P(A\cap B)=0.$

We can calculate $P(A\cap B)$ using the addition law:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ 0.8 & =0.25+0.75-P(A\cap B) \\ P(A\cap B) & =0.25+0.75-0.8 \\  & =0.2\ne 0.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Determining Whether Two Events are Mutually Exclusive
content.problem: Given $P(A)=0.25$, $P(B)=0.75$, $P(A\cup B)=0.8$, determine whether  $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events.
content.worked_solution:
To check if $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, we must check that $P(A\cap B)=0.$

We can calculate $P(A\cap B)$ using the addition law:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ 0.8 & =0.25+0.75-P(A\cap B) \\ P(A\cap B) & =0.25+0.75-0.8 \\  & =0.2\ne 0.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A$ and $B$ are not mutually exclusive events.

Given P(A)=38, P(B)=13, and P(A∪B)=1724, determine whether A and B are mutually exclusive events.

a
A and B are mutually exclusive events, since P(A∩B)=0

A and B are not mutually exclusive events, since P(A)≠P(B)
e

decision.explanation: Using the addition law, P(A∩B)=3/8+1/3−17/24=9/24+8/24−17/24=0. Therefore, A and B are mutually exclusive.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Given $P(A)=\frac{3}{8},$ $P(B)=\frac{1}{3},$ and $P(A\cup B)=\frac{17}{24},$ determine whether $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events.
after.worked_solution:
To check if $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, we must check that $P(A\cap B)=0.$

We can calculate $P(A\cap B)$ using the addition law:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ \frac{17}{24} & =\frac{3}{8}+\frac{1}{3}-P(A\cap B) \\ P(A\cap B) & =\frac{3}{8}+\frac{1}{3}-\frac{17}{24} \\  & =\frac{9+8-17}{24} \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events.

a
A and B are mutually exclusive events, since P(A∩B)=0
b
A and B are not mutually exclusive events, since P(A∩B)≠0

A and B are not mutually exclusive events, since P(A)⋅P(B)≠P(A∪B)

A and B are not mutually exclusive events, since P(A)⋅P(B)<P(A∪B)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To check if A and B are mutually exclusive, we must check that P(A∩B)=0.

We can calculate P(A∩B) using the addition law: P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)1724=38+13−P(A∩B)P(A∩B)=38+13−1724=9+8−1724=0✓ Therefore, A and B are mutually exclusive events.

content.knowledge_point: Determining Whether Two Events are Mutually Exclusive
content.problem: Given $P(A)=\frac{3}{8},$ $P(B)=\frac{1}{3},$ and $P(A\cup B)=\frac{17}{24},$ determine whether $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events.
content.worked_solution:
To check if $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, we must check that $P(A\cap B)=0.$

We can calculate $P(A\cap B)$ using the addition law:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ \frac{17}{24} & =\frac{3}{8}+\frac{1}{3}-P(A\cap B) \\ P(A\cap B) & =\frac{3}{8}+\frac{1}{3}-\frac{17}{24} \\  & =\frac{9+8-17}{24} \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events.

Given P(A)=14, P(B)=310, and P(A∪B)=1940, determine whether A and B are mutually exclusive events.

a
A and B are not mutually exclusive events, since P(A)⋅P(B)<P(A∪B)
b
A and B are not mutually exclusive events, since P(A)⋅P(B)≠P(A∪B)
c
A and B are not mutually exclusive events, since P(A∩B)≠0
d
A and B are not mutually exclusive events, since P(A)≠P(B)
e
A and B are mutually exclusive events, since P(A∩B)=0

decision.explanation: By the addition law, P(A∩B)=1/4+3/10−19/40=(10+12−19)/40=3/40≠0. Therefore, A and B are not mutually exclusive.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Given $P(A)=\frac{1}{4},$ $P(B)=\frac{3}{10},$ and $P(A\cup B)=\frac{19}{40},$ determine whether $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events.
after.worked_solution:
To check if $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, we must check that $P(A\cap B)=0.$

We can calculate $P(A\cap B)$ using the addition law:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ \frac{19}{40} & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{3}{10}-P(A\cap B) \\ P(A\cap B) & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{3}{10}-\frac{19}{40} \\  & =\frac{10+12-19}{40} \\  & =\frac{3}{40} \\  & \ne 0\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A$ and $B$ are not mutually exclusive events.

content.problem: Given $P(A)=\frac{1}{4},$ $P(B)=\frac{3}{10},$ and $P(A\cup B)=\frac{19}{40},$ determine whether $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events.
content.worked_solution:
To check if $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, we must check that $P(A\cap B)=0.$

We can calculate $P(A\cap B)$ using the addition law:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ \frac{19}{40} & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{3}{10}-P(A\cap B) \\ P(A\cap B) & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{3}{10}-\frac{19}{40} \\  & =\frac{10+12-19}{40} \\  & =\frac{3}{40} \\  & \ne 0\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A$ and $B$ are not mutually exclusive events.

content.problem: Given $P(A)=\frac{1}{3}$, $P(B)=\frac{3}{8}$, $P(A\cup B)=\frac{17}{24}$, determine whether $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events.
content.worked_solution:
To check if $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, we must check that $P(A\cap B)=0.$

We can calculate $P(A\cap B)$ using the addition law:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ \frac{17}{24} & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{3}{8}-P(A\cap B) \\ P(A\cap B) & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{3}{8}-\frac{17}{24} \\  & =\frac{8+9-17}{24}=0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Given $P(A)=\frac{2}{7},$ $P(B)=\frac{1}{3},$ and $P(A\cup B)=\frac{10}{21},$ determine whether $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events.
after.worked_solution:
To check if $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, we must check that $P(A\cap B)=0.$

We can calculate $P(A\cap B)$ using the addition law:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ \frac{10}{21} & =\frac{2}{7}+\frac{1}{3}-P(A\cap B) \\ P(A\cap B) & =\frac{2}{7}+\frac{1}{3}-\frac{10}{21} \\  & =\frac{6+7-10}{21} \\  & =\frac{1}{7} \\  & \ne 0\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A$ and $B$ are not mutually exclusive events.

Given P(A)=27, P(B)=13, and P(A∪B)=1021, determine whether A and B are mutually exclusive events.

a
A and B are not mutually exclusive events, since P(A∩B)≠0
b
A and B are not mutually exclusive events, since P(A)⋅P(B)<P(A∪B)
c
A and B are mutually exclusive events, since P(A∩B)=0
d
A and B are not mutually exclusive events, since P(A)⋅P(B)≠P(A∪B)
e
A and B are not mutually exclusive events, since P(A)≠P(B)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To check if A and B are mutually exclusive, we must check that P(A∩B)=0.

We can calculate P(A∩B) using the addition law: P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)1021=27+13−P(A∩B)P(A∩B)=27+13−1021=6+7−1021=17≠0× Therefore, A and B are not mutually exclusive events.

content.knowledge_point: Determining Whether Two Events are Mutually Exclusive
content.problem: Given $P(A)=\frac{2}{7},$ $P(B)=\frac{1}{3},$ and $P(A\cup B)=\frac{10}{21},$ determine whether $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events.
content.worked_solution:
To check if $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, we must check that $P(A\cap B)=0.$

We can calculate $P(A\cap B)$ using the addition law:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ \frac{10}{21} & =\frac{2}{7}+\frac{1}{3}-P(A\cap B) \\ P(A\cap B) & =\frac{2}{7}+\frac{1}{3}-\frac{10}{21} \\  & =\frac{6+7-10}{21} \\  & =\frac{1}{7} \\  & \ne 0\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A$ and $B$ are not mutually exclusive events.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events. Given that $P(B)=\frac{1}{15}$ and $P(A\cup B)=\frac{3}{5},$ find $P(A).$
after.worked_solution:
If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events, then $P(A\cap B)=0.$ 

Therefore, by the addition law, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B) \\ P(A) & =P(A\cup B)-P(B) \\  & =\frac{3}{5}-\frac{1}{15} \\  & =\frac{9-1}{15} \\  & =\frac{8}{15}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events. Given that $P(A)=\frac{2}{7}$ and $P(A\cup B)=\frac{3}{4},$ find $P(B).$
after.worked_solution:
If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events, then $P(A\cap B)=0.$

Therefore, by the addition law, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B) \\ P(B) & =P(A\cup B)-P(A) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}-\frac{2}{7} \\  & =\frac{21-8}{28} \\  & =\frac{13}{28}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Computing a Probability Involving Mutually Exclusive Events
content.problem: Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events. Given that $P(A)=\frac{2}{7}$ and $P(A\cup B)=\frac{3}{4},$ find $P(B).$
content.worked_solution:
If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events, then $P(A\cap B)=0.$

Therefore, by the addition law, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B) \\ P(B) & =P(A\cup B)-P(A) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}-\frac{2}{7} \\  & =\frac{21-8}{28} \\  & =\frac{13}{28}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events. Given that $P(B)=\frac{8}{21}$ and $P(A\cup B)=\frac{3}{4},$ find $P(A).$
after.worked_solution:
If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events, then $P(A\cap B)=0.$ 

Therefore, by the addition law, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B) \\ P(A) & =P(A\cup B)-P(B) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}-\frac{8}{21} \\  & =\frac{63-32}{84} \\  & =\frac{31}{84}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: White and green are mutually exclusive outcomes. There are 3+15=18 favorable panels out of 50, so the probability is 18/50=9/25.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: A game show uses a roulette wheel divided into $50$ panels. There are $15$ blue, $15$ green, $15$ yellow, $2$ black, and $3$ white panels randomly shuffled on the roulette wheel. What is the probability that the roulette wheel stops on a white or green panel?
after.worked_solution:
Let $W$ be the event that the roulette will stop on a white panel, and let $G$ be the event that the roulette will stop on a green panel. Then the probability that the roulette stops on a white or green panel given by $P(W\cup G).$

Given that the roulette will stop at only one panel, the events $W$ and $G$  are mutually exclusive, i.e., $P(W\cap G)=0.$ 

We can find $P(W)$ and $P(G)$ by computing the necessary ratios. There are $50$ panels in the roulette. Of those panels, $3$ are white, and $15$ are green. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W) & =\frac{3}{50}. \\ P(G) & =\frac{15}{50}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by the addition law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W\cup G) & =P(W)+P(G)-P(W\cap G) \\  & =\frac{3}{50}+\frac{15}{50}-0 \\  & =\frac{18}{50} \\  & =\frac{9}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 11
?

A game show uses a roulette wheel divided into 50 panels. There are 15 blue, 15 green, 15 yellow, 2 black, and 3 white panels randomly shuffled on the roulette wheel. What is the probability that the roulette wheel stops on a white or green panel?

a
1825
b
325
c
625
d
925
e
950
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let W be the event that the roulette will stop on a white panel, and let G be the event that the roulette will stop on a green panel. Then the probability that the roulette stops on a white or green panel given by P(W∪G).

Given that the roulette will stop at only one panel, the events W and G are mutually exclusive, i.e., P(W∩G)=0.

We can find P(W) and P(G) by computing the necessary ratios. There are 50 panels in the roulette. Of those panels, 3 are white, and 15 are green. Therefore,

P(W)=350.P(G)=1550.

Finally, by the addition law, we have

P(W∪G)=P(W)+P(G)−P(W∩G)=350+1550−0=1850=925.

content.knowledge_point: Computing a Probability Involving Mutually Exclusive Events: Word Problems
content.problem: A game show uses a roulette wheel divided into $50$ panels. There are $15$ blue, $15$ green, $15$ yellow, $2$ black, and $3$ white panels randomly shuffled on the roulette wheel. What is the probability that the roulette wheel stops on a white or green panel?
content.worked_solution:
Let $W$ be the event that the roulette will stop on a white panel, and let $G$ be the event that the roulette will stop on a green panel. Then the probability that the roulette stops on a white or green panel given by $P(W\cup G).$

Given that the roulette will stop at only one panel, the events $W$ and $G$  are mutually exclusive, i.e., $P(W\cap G)=0.$ 

We can find $P(W)$ and $P(G)$ by computing the necessary ratios. There are $50$ panels in the roulette. Of those panels, $3$ are white, and $15$ are green. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W) & =\frac{3}{50}. \\ P(G) & =\frac{15}{50}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by the addition law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W\cup G) & =P(W)+P(G)-P(W\cap G) \\  & =\frac{3}{50}+\frac{15}{50}-0 \\  & =\frac{18}{50} \\  & =\frac{9}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: After removing the Ace of Spades, 51 cards remain: 3 aces and 12 spades, with no overlap. The probability is (3+12)/51=15/51=5/17.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
A card is drawn from a standard $52$-card deck. The drawn card is the Ace of Spades and it is set aside. A second card is drawn from the deck. What is the probability that the drawn card is an ace or a spade?

*Hint: A standard $52$-card deck has $4$ suits with $13$ cards in each suit. Spades is one of the suits.*
after.worked_solution:
Let us call $A$ the event "The second card drawn is an ace," and $S$ the event "The second card drawn is a spade." The required probability is given by  $P(A\cup S).$ 

Given that the Ace of Spades is no longer in the deck, $A$ and $S$ are mutually exclusive events, i.e., $P(A\cap S)=0.$

Since the Ace of Spades was set aside, there are $51$ cards remaining,  of which $3$ are aces and $12$ are spades. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =\frac{3}{51}, \\ P(S) & =\frac{12}{51}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by the addition law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup S) & =P(A)+P(S)-P(A\cap S) \\  & =\frac{3}{51}+\frac{12}{51}-0 \\  & =\frac{3+12}{51} \\  & =\frac{15}{51} \\  & =\frac{5}{17}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Computing a Probability Involving Mutually Exclusive Events: Word Problems
content.problem:
A card is drawn from a standard $52$-card deck. The drawn card is the Ace of Spades and it is set aside. A second card is drawn from the deck. What is the probability that the drawn card is an ace or a spade?

*Hint: A standard $52$-card deck has $4$ suits with $13$ cards in each suit. Spades is one of the suits.*
content.worked_solution:
Let us call $A$ the event "The second card drawn is an ace," and $S$ the event "The second card drawn is a spade." The required probability is given by  $P(A\cup S).$ 

Given that the Ace of Spades is no longer in the deck, $A$ and $S$ are mutually exclusive events, i.e., $P(A\cap S)=0.$

Since the Ace of Spades was set aside, there are $51$ cards remaining,  of which $3$ are aces and $12$ are spades. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =\frac{3}{51}, \\ P(S) & =\frac{12}{51}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by the addition law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup S) & =P(A)+P(S)-P(A\cap S) \\  & =\frac{3}{51}+\frac{12}{51}-0 \\  & =\frac{3+12}{51} \\  & =\frac{15}{51} \\  & =\frac{5}{17}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 13
after.problem: A number is picked from $10$ to $19.$ What is the probability of picking an even number or a prime number?
after.worked_solution:
Let $E$ be the event that the picked number is an even number, and let $R$ be the event that the picked number is a prime number. Then the probability that the selected number is an even number or a prime number is $P(E\cup R).$

Given that all prime numbers between $10$ and $19$ are odd, $E$ and $R$ are mutually exclusive events, i.e., $P(E\cap R)=0.$

We can find $P(E)$ and $P(R)$ by computing the necessary ratios. There are $10$ numbers from  $10$ to $19$, of which  $5$ are even, and $4$ are prime.   Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(E) & =\frac{5}{10} \\ P(R) & =\frac{4}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by the addition law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(E\cup R) & =P(E)+P(R)-P(E\cap R) \\  & =\frac{5}{10}+\frac{4}{10}-0 \\  & =\frac{9}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Let E be the event that the picked number is an even number, and let R be the event that the picked number is a prime number. Then the probability that the selected number is an even number or a prime number is P(E∪R).

Given that all prime numbers between 10 and 19 are odd, E and R are mutually exclusive events, i.e., P(E∩R)=0.

We can find P(E) and P(R) by computing the necessary ratios. There are 10 numbers from 10 to 19, of which 5 are even, and 4 are prime. Therefore:

P(E)=510P(R)=410.

Finally, by the addition law, we have

P(E∪R)=P(E)+P(R)−P(E∩R)=510+410−0=910.

after.name: Question 14
after.problem: On a shelf, there are $11$ novels and $9$ science books. $1$ of the novels and $3$ of the science books are illustrated. The illustrated novel is taken from the shelf and set apart. If a single book is selected at random, what is the probability that it is a novel or an illustrated book?
after.worked_solution:
Let $I$ be the event that the selected book is an illustrated book, and let $N$ be the event that it is a novel. Then the probability that the selected book is a novel or an illustrated book is given by $P(I\cup N).$

Since the only illustrated novel was removed, there are no novels left on the shelf that are also illustrated. Therefore, $I$ and $N$ are mutually exclusive events, i.e., $P(I\cap N)=0.$

Since the illustrated novel was set apart, there are $10+9=19$ books remaining, of which $10$ are novels and $3$ are illustrated. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(I) & =\frac{3}{19}, \\ P(N) & =\frac{10}{19}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by the addition law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(I\cup N) & =P(I)+P(N)-P(I\cap N) \\  & =\frac{3}{19}+\frac{10}{19}-0 \\  & =\frac{3+10}{19} \\  & =\frac{13}{19}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 15
after.problem: Kevin is choosing a random name for his new character in a video game. If all names may only start with an uppercase letter, what is the probability that the generated name will start with an "R" or an "E"?
after.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be the event that the name starts with an "R," and let $E$ be the event that the name starts with an "E." Then the probability that the name will start with an "R" or an "E" is given by $P(R\cup E).$

Given that only one letter can be picked as the first letter, $R$ and $E$ are mutually exclusive events. i.e. $P(R\cap E)=0.$

There are $26$ letters in the alphabet, and each letter has an equal chance of being randomly picked ($1$ out of $26$). Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(R) & =\frac{1}{26}, \\ P(E) & =\frac{1}{26}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by the addition law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(R\cup E) & =P(R)+P(E)-P(R\cap E) \\  & =\frac{1}{26}+\frac{1}{26}-0 \\  & =\frac{2}{26} \\  & =\frac{1}{13}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15

Kevin is choosing a random name for his new character in a video game. If all names may only start with an uppercase letter, what is the probability that the generated name will start with an "R" or an "E"?

a
126
b
313
c
326
d
113
e
213
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let R be the event that the name starts with an "R," and let E be the event that the name starts with an "E." Then the probability that the name will start with an "R" or an "E" is given by P(R∪E).

Given that only one letter can be picked as the first letter, R and E are mutually exclusive events. i.e. P(R∩E)=0.

There are 26 letters in the alphabet, and each letter has an equal chance of being randomly picked (1 out of 26). Therefore,

P(R)=126,P(E)=126.

Finally, by the addition law, we have P(R∪E)=P(R)+P(E)−P(R∩E)=126+126−0=226=113.

content.problem: Kevin is choosing a random name for his new character in a video game. If all names may only start with an uppercase letter, what is the probability that the generated name will start with an "R" or an "E"?
content.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be the event that the name starts with an "R," and let $E$ be the event that the name starts with an "E." Then the probability that the name will start with an "R" or an "E" is given by $P(R\cup E).$

Given that only one letter can be picked as the first letter, $R$ and $E$ are mutually exclusive events. i.e. $P(R\cap E)=0.$

There are $26$ letters in the alphabet, and each letter has an equal chance of being randomly picked ($1$ out of $26$). Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(R) & =\frac{1}{26}, \\ P(E) & =\frac{1}{26}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by the addition law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(R\cup E) & =P(R)+P(E)-P(R\cap E) \\  & =\frac{1}{26}+\frac{1}{26}-0 \\  & =\frac{2}{26} \\  & =\frac{1}{13}.\end{aligned}
$$
